10. Comparability Over Time and Space

Observed data collection methods and processing algorithms have been applied consistently over time and space. NASA’s satellites cover the entire area of interest except for the “pole hole” described above. Even though the size of this hole has changed over time as a result of different satellites with slightly different orbits and coverage, EPA’s indicator uses a data set that corrects for this discontinuity.

GCMs inherently use consistent algorithms over time and space.

The observed and projected time series cover the same spatial extent: all sea ice in the Northern Hemisphere, which, in September, is limited to the Arctic region. Observed and projected series reflect the same indicator definition, but they are fundamentally based on different pixel sizes for analysis, as described in Section 7 above.

11. Data Limitations

The technical documentation for the Arctic Sea Ice indicator identifies some factors that may impact the confidence, application, or conclusions that readers can draw from the observed portion of this pairing. The documentation acknowledges natural variability in sea ice that might not be driven by climate, for example, and it notes that satellite data collection is generally accurate but not an exact accounting.

Future projections of any variable have inherent uncertainty, as described in Section 12 below. Sea ice is influenced by multiple systems and processes, so it may be less direct to model than, say, surface air temperature.

12. Sources of Uncertainty

Observations inevitably reflect measurement uncertainty. NSIDC has calculated standard deviations along with each monthly ice concentration average. NSIDC’s Sea Ice Index documentation describes several analyses that have examined the accuracy and uncertainty of passive microwave imagery and the NASA Team algorithm used to create this indicator. For example, a 1991 analysis estimated that ice concentrations measured by passive microwave imagery are accurate to within 5 to 9 percent, depending on the ice being imaged. Another study suggested that the NASA Team algorithm underestimates ice extent by 4 percent in the winter, and more in summer months. A third study that compared the NASA Team algorithm with new, higher-resolution data found that the NASA Team algorithm underestimates ice extent by an average of 10 percent. For more details and study citations, see NSIDC’s Sea Ice Index. Certain ice conditions, particularly thin or melting ice, can lead to larger errors. For example, a melt pond on an ice floe might be mapped as open water. The instruments also can have difficulty distinguishing the interface between ice and snow or a diffuse boundary between ice and open water. Using the September minimum minimizes many of these effects, because melt ponds and the ice surface have largely begun to refreeze by then. These errors do not affect trends and relative changes from year to year.

Model outputs inevitably reflect model uncertainty. Each GCM represents aspects of, and processes within, the climate system differently. These differences will lead to differences in how the GCMs represent both present-day climate and how the climate responds to changes in greenhouse gases. For example, GCMs differ in climate sensitivity, defined as the increase in global temperature when carbon dioxide in the atmosphere doubles relative to pre-industrial times. Even a single GCM will yield different results if presented with different initial conditions, as the chaotic processes within the model will lead to different timing of various modes of variability within the model (such as the El Niño cycle). The shaded bands in the graph for this pairing illustrate this type of uncertainty in the spread of models, as well as year-to-year variations due to internal variability within each model.

Interpreting projections also requires users to consider scenario uncertainty. Projecting future conditions requires assumptions about future greenhouse gas emissions. This feature presents four widely used scenarios to illustrate a range of possibilities without assigning likelihoods to them, nor do these scenarios necessarily bound possible futures.

13. Sources of Variability

As the technical documentation for the Arctic Sea Ice indicator explains, the apparent extent of sea ice can vary widely from day to day, both due to real variability in ice extent (growth, melting, and movement of ice at the edge of the ice pack) and due to ephemeral effects such as weather, clouds and water vapor, melt on the ice surface, and changes in the character of the snow and ice surface. The indicator documentation also discusses variability associated with weather patterns and year-to-year oscillations in atmospheric circulation. The construction of this pairing addresses variability in a few ways:

  • Using extent rather than area, as NSIDC has determined that extent is a more stable variable, although area could be less sensitive to resolution .
  • Using monthly averages to reduce some of the day-to-day “noise” inherent in daily sea ice measurements.
  • Smoothing GCM outputs with an 11-year moving average.
